title: A Fun Way To Improve Group Work Participation https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/09/03/a-fun-way-to-improve-group-work-participation/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a step-by-step activity, the 'decision game,' for teachers whose students disengage from group work despite thorough modeling and clear expectations. The game groups students of four or five facing each other, poses a quick fun question (favorite ice cream, scariest movie character), gives the group 8-10 seconds to agree on one answer, and awards points based on full participation and answer originality, with zero points if the group fails to answer in unison. He walks through each step precisely, including how to handle a refusing student without singling them out ('just tell them to let you know when they're ready to rejoin'), and stresses that the points themselves are meaningless — the value lies purely in the low-stakes fun that gets students accustomed to contributing. He recommends it especially at the start of the year, framing it as a fast, playful way to convert reluctant participants into eager ones over just a few rounds.
points: The 'decision game' groups students of four or five and has them agree on and call out a single answer to a fun question within 8-10 seconds.
Points are awarded for full-group participation and answer originality, with zero points if the group fails to answer in unison — but the points themselves are described as meaningless.
A student who refuses to participate should be quietly allowed to sit and watch until ready, without being singled out as 'in trouble.'
The game works by exerting gentle, positive peer pressure to cooperate rather than through lecturing or reteaching group-work expectations.
It is recommended especially at the start of the school year as a fast way to convert reluctant participants into eager ones.
quotes: Well, you can reteach. But you already taught your expectations thoroughly, so repeating the lesson is unlikely to make a difference.
Break students up into groups of four or five so they’re facing each other.
Assign five points per group for full participation (in calling out their answer) and an original answer (an answer no other group gave).
If someone does refuse, gently ask them to sit off to the side and watch until they feel more comfortable. (They’re not “in trouble.” Just tell them to let you know when they’re ready to rejoin.)
As for points, they’re absolutely meaningless. The winning group gets bragging rights, nothing more.
Done right, the game will help leapfrog your class—sometimes by weeks—from grudging and reluctant participants . . . To happy and eager contributors.
